scenes.visual: Title card 'Reading the DNA Rung' over the top rung of the evidence ladder glowing gold. COLOUR MAP (both films): mushroom card PURPLE #8a5a9e, oak card GREEN #2e8b4f, deer card BROWN #a0662b, paramecium card TEAL #0e7c86, bacterium card ORANGE #d0701a, archaeon card CRIMSON #b23b4e (the lesson's simulation colours). Each card is a flat cartoon of the organism with its name underneath, on a white card with a thick left edge in its colour. The EVIDENCE LADDER stands at the left edge, four rungs bottom to top: 'eyes', 'microscope', 'cell chemistry', 'DNA'; the current rung glows gold. Domain boxes are labelled 'Bacteria', 'Archaea', 'Eukarya' in that order left to right, charcoal outlines. All cells are cartoons labelled 'schematic'. In this film, building blocks of a protein are round BEADS in five muted colours; a matching position lights GOLD, a non-matching one stays grey.

scenes.tts: Cell clues and feeding showed that a mushroom is not a plant. They cannot show who its closest relatives are. How could the cells' own instructions tell you?
scenes.visual: The mushroom card sits alone in its 'Fungi' box. Dotted lines reach toward the oak card and the deer card, each with a '?'. A strand of DNA unspools from the mushroom card.
scenes.narration: Cell clues and feeding showed that a mushroom is not a plant. They cannot show who its closest relatives are. How could the cells' own instructions tell you?

scenes.tts: The first film climbed three rungs of the evidence ladder. Now climb the top rung, DNA, with the same six cards.
scenes.visual: Brief replay: the first film's ladder with 'eyes', 'microscope' and 'cell chemistry' ticked, and the three domain boxes 'Bacteria', 'Archaea', 'Eukarya' with the six cards in place. The 'DNA' rung glows.
scenes.narration: The first film climbed three rungs of the evidence ladder. Now climb the top rung, DNA, with the same six cards.

scenes.tts: The order of the chemical letters in a stretch of DNA is its DNA sequence. Each protein is built from a gene's instructions. So comparing proteins is another way to compare genes.
scenes.visual: A DNA strand with letters A, C, G, T scrolling along it, label 'DNA sequence'. An arrow from a highlighted stretch labelled 'gene' points to a chain of beads labelled 'protein (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: The order of the chemical letters in a stretch of DNA is its DNA sequence. Each protein is built from a gene's instructions. So comparing proteins is another way to compare genes.

scenes.tts: A protein is a chain of building blocks called amino acids. To compare, line up the same protein from two living things. Each place in the line is a position. At each position, the building blocks match, or they do not.
scenes.caption: A protein is a chain of building blocks called amino acids. To compare, line up the same protein from two living things. Each place in the line is a position. At each position, the building blocks match, or they do not.
scenes.visual: Two bead chains slide in from left and right and line up one above the other. A bracket marks one column, labelled 'position'. Columns where the two beads are the same colour light GOLD; others stay grey.
scenes.narration: A protein is a chain of building blocks called amino acids. To compare, line up the same protein from two living things. Each place in the line is a position. At each position, the building blocks match, or they do not.

scenes.tts: Here is a made-up example, only ten building blocks long. Line up living thing A with living thing B, and count the matches. Then line up A with C.
scenes.visual: Label 'made-up example' in the corner. Three ten-bead chains labelled 'A', 'B', 'C' in neutral grey card frames (not the organism colours). A over B: 8 columns light gold, counter shows '8 of 10'. A over C: 6 columns light gold, counter shows '6 of 10'.
scenes.narration: Here is a made-up example, only ten building blocks long. Line up living thing A with living thing B, and count the matches. Then line up A with C.

scenes.tts: A matches B more closely in this one protein. That is one clue that A and B may share a more recent common ancestor. That is an organism both groups descend from.
scenes.visual: Two bars grow side by side: 'A and B' longer than 'A and C', labelled 'made-up'. A small DASHED family tree sketches itself: A and B join at a nearer fork, C joins farther down. The near fork is labelled 'more recent common ancestor?' and the whole sketch carries a tag 'one clue: a guess to test'. Do not draw it as a settled tree.
scenes.narration: A matches B more closely in this one protein. That is one clue that A and B may share a more recent common ancestor. That is an organism both groups descend from.

scenes.tts: But a match count is a clue, not proof. One group's version can change faster than another's. So scientists build family trees from many genes before they trust a grouping.
scenes.visual: The two bars shrink to nearly equal length; a label reads 'one protein: a clue'. Then a stack of many bar pairs, one per gene, slides in and feeds into a small family tree, labelled 'many genes agree'.
scenes.narration: But a match count is a clue, not proof. One group's version can change faster than another's. So scientists build family trees from many genes before they trust a grouping.

scenes.tts: In 1993, Sandra Baldauf and Jeffrey Palmer looked at twenty-five proteins from animals, fungi, plants and other living things. One protein is called E F one alpha.
scenes.caption: In 1993, Sandra Baldauf and Jeffrey Palmer looked at 25 proteins from animals, fungi, plants and other living things. One protein is called EF-1 alpha.
scenes.visual: On-screen text '1993: Baldauf and Palmer', '25 proteins'. Three long bead chains labelled 'animal' (BROWN frame), 'fungus' (PURPLE frame), 'plant' (GREEN frame), with the label 'EF-1 alpha (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: In 1993, Sandra Baldauf and Jeffrey Palmer looked at 25 proteins from animals, fungi, plants and other living things. One protein is called EF-1 alpha.

scenes.tts: In this protein, the animals and fungi they studied share an extra stretch, twelve building blocks long. Do the plants have it too? Decide what each answer would mean.
scenes.caption: In this protein, the animals and fungi they studied share an extra stretch, 12 building blocks long. Do the plants have it too? Decide what each answer would mean.
scenes.visual: In the animal and fungus chains, a run of 12 beads lights up in the same spot, labelled '12 extra building blocks'. The plant chain at that spot is hidden behind a card marked '?'.
scenes.narration: In this protein, the animals and fungi they studied share an extra stretch, 12 building blocks long. Do the plants have it too? Decide what each answer would mean.

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The '?' card over the plant chain holds; a 5-second ring timer runs at bottom right.

scenes.tts: The plants did not have it. The simplest story is one change, in an ancestor that animals and fungi share but plants do not. And all four proteins they used to draw family trees grouped animals with fungi.
scenes.visual: The '?' card flips: the plant chain has a gap where the 12 beads would be. A small family tree grows: one fork gives the animal and fungus branches, and the extra stretch appears as a gold mark on the stem just below that fork. The plant branch splits off lower down. On-screen: '4 of 4 trees: animals with fungi'.
scenes.narration: The plants did not have it. The simplest story is one change, in an ancestor that animals and fungi share but plants do not. And all four proteins they used to draw family trees grouped animals with fungi.

scenes.tts: So the evidence supports this tree. Fungi and animals sit on neighbouring branches. Plants sit farther off. Fungi and animals share a more recent common ancestor than either shares with plants. Many other proteins agree.
scenes.visual: The six cards from the first film snap onto the tree: mushroom (PURPLE) and deer (BROWN) on neighbouring branches, oak (GREEN) farther off, all inside a box labelled 'Eukarya'. Labelled 'schematic tree'. A small stack of gene icons beside the tree is labelled 'many other proteins agree'.
scenes.narration: So the evidence supports this tree. Fungi and animals sit on neighbouring branches. Plants sit farther off. Fungi and animals share a more recent common ancestor than either shares with plants. Many other proteins agree.

scenes.tts: One last warning. A closer relative is not the same kind. Fungi are closer to animals, but a mushroom is still not an animal. Closer means a more recent common ancestor.
scenes.visual: The mushroom card and the deer card stand side by side on the tree. A caption appears: 'closer relative' with a crossed-out 'same kind'. The mushroom stays in its own 'Fungi' box.
scenes.narration: One last warning. A closer relative is not the same kind. Fungi are closer to animals, but a mushroom is still not an animal. Closer means a more recent common ancestor.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex mascot. Line: 'When many genes agree, they point to a more recent common ancestor.'
